utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Call the case, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, Monday, the 24th of August, 2009, I would like to greet Mr. Praljak, Mr. Pusic, who has returned, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic. I would like to greet the Defence counsel and Mr. Stringer, who is currently conducting his cross-examination. And I wouldn't like to forget to greet everyone else assisting us. Mr. Stringer, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, when we left off last week on Thursday, we were looking at P04142. And I see that you don't have the binder there with you, and I would be grateful if the -- it's list 5. It's the -- yeah, I believe we're now into the second binder, General, the smaller one. This was P04142.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's in the second large one. I can't find it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in the larger binder, the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It might be the last document in the first binder. The number again is 4142. Okay, I see that you have the document now, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to recap, this is a training programme for HVO conscripts that was issued shortly after you took command of the HVO Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And last week, when we were talking about this, we were talking about the section on homeland education, and I was asking you about the various topics that fell within the training on homeland education, and so I'd just like to continue with that now. Do you have -- let me give you a page reference that you can go to, General. In your version, if you would turn to the page that ends with the number 0839, which is page 14 of the English version. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we talked about some of these parts already, so that I'm going to skip over them so that we don't repeat. So I'm going to continue -- if you actually continue looking down, then, you have various topics which are identified. I'm looking at page 16 of the English. There's topic number 1 and then topic number 2, relating to Greater Serbian claims to Croatian lands. And then topic number 3 has to do with the history of Croatian people and Croatian lands. This is now on page 17 of the English. So, General, just to get back to where we were, I'm looking at topic 3, and since this is a training programme for the HVO, which is very actively involved in military activities throughout the territory of the HZ-HB at this period of time, late summer of 1993, what we see here are many references to Croatian people, Croatian culture, Croatian history in these areas, and no reference at all to any of the other peoples who were inhabiting the areas of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; isn't that true? No reference to Muslims, for example, or even the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with that, Mr. Stringer. Under item 1, there's an introduction to the history, the background of towns and regions. Under 2, Greater Serbian claims to Croatian lands, and then details are given about the books that deal with the subject. Then, naturally, there's the -- there are more subjects about the Croatian people. There's more information about the Croatian people, because given the history as it is, you can't study the history of the Croats if you don't include the history of the other peoples who lived in the same area. When dealing with these subjects, subject 3, for example, it says very explicitly "Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn the page or move to the next topic, topic number 4, which is on page 18 of the English. Now, topic number 4 is entitled "Role and Importance of Church in the Lives of Croatian People," and this aspect of the homeland training for HVO conscripts involves the christening of the Croats, the acceptance of the Pope as the superior moral and spiritual authority, struggle for the Croatian language, Croatian martyrs and saints. I'm just moving down. General, it seems quite clear, wouldn't you agree, that based on this aspect of the training programme, your intent is that the HVO, your HVO, is not a secular armed forces, but is, in fact, a religious armed forces or has a strongly religious orientation which, of course, is toward the Catholic Church?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's completely wrong, Mr. Stringer. The topics here starts with the christening of Croats who arrived in the area in the 8th and 9th centuries. It has to do with accepting the authority of the Pope, and that goes back to the 10th or 11th century, in the case of the Croats. So this is history, such as it was, and in every Western European country you can't study history if you do not at the same time study the religion practiced in the church. The night of the St. Bartholomew can't be interpreted if one isn't aware of the relationship with the Inugonauts [phoen] and the Catholics and the Pope and so on and so forth. So here you have a reference to the Bogomils as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There is a reference at the end of this to other religious influences, and as you point out, you've identified the Bogomils as well as the Islam and Orthodox religion, which were the religions of the Muslims and the Serbs there, but in fact this is quite clearly a programme which is intended to indoctrinate HVO soldiers in a way that would suggest that they are Christian or Catholic fighters as members of the HVO, isn't that true, with the other religions merely having an influence on history, but no real -- certainly no orientation or neutrality within the HVO in respect of religion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir. In Croatia, where the first mosque in the Balkans was constructed at the time -- before the Second World War -- well, this is completely false. The 28 topics listed here -- the 28 books listed here, well, we wanted to correct some falsehood with regard to history, but there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll get to the books in a moment. In terms of this training programme, however, doesn't this indicate that an HVO conscript is being trained or is somehow required or pressured to accept the Pope of the Roman Catholic Church as the superior, moral, and spiritual authority? That seems very clear on its face, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not clear on its face, not even when you go back to the issue. It's about history, and you study history by studying historical facts. What you have said isn't contained anywhere. This is not how matters were understood. To accept the Pope as an authority, in the case of the Catholic Church, goes back to the 10th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And my point, though, is that the HVO and the conscripts and soldiers of the HVO were apparently supposed to accept the Pope as the superior moral authority as well. Isn't that true? Weren't they trained in this way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct, sir. Croatia, from the very outset, was a secular state. The HZ-HB is a secular organisation. It was part of saving Bosnia and Herzegovina. But what you have said isn't referred to anywhere. This is not how one proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I'm going to continue on, and on page 19 of the English now there's a reference to Croatian and Herceg-Bosna as one geo-strategic entity, and we spoke about that item last week. It was raised initially by the President, and then I followed up, so I'm not going to go back to that now. I think we covered it last week sufficiently. But we can, as you've suggested, General, just take a very brief moment to look at the reading list or the suggested literature that you've referred to, which is found on page 20. And I'm not going to go through this list in any detail other than to again put to you, General, that the message here is that the -- a Croat soldier -- or, excuse me, an HVO soldier is a soldier who, in your HVO, is going to be a Croat soldier who's going to have a solid grasp of Croat culture, history, and the role of Croats in this region, and then it's essentially an HVO which excludes other groups such as Muslims, other religions such as Islam. Isn't that true? The HVO is to be an exclusively Croat-oriented military?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's false, sir. Under item 5, reference is made to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the war in Croatia, so it refers to two states. The current situation, on the Croatian and Bosnian-Herzegovinian battle-fields. The HVO soldier was taught that these were two states, and naturally there was a clear strategic link between those two wars. So this is a subject I have discussed at length. And, sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I quite simply don't understand where you draw such conclusions from. I completely disagree with such conclusions because they are erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you disagree with me, General, then, if I suggest to you that your vision of the HVO, as set out in this training programme, is one that excludes any possibility of a multi-ethnic armed forces? Isn't that your vision of the HVO, as set out here, a mono-ethnic armed force, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That was never the case for the HVO. The information we have provided the Court with quite clearly demonstrate that the HVO was the only real multi-ethnic military force in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But not in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say the HVO, wherever the HVO was, well, it was multi-ethnic from the very beginning to the end; naturally, a little less so after the ABiH launched the attack it launched and betrayed the course, but it didn't lose its multi-ethnic character. At the time, wherever the HVO was in existence, it was open to the Muslims and to the Serbs as well. There was such cases, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll talk about this again later, General. But the fact is that throughout the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone and the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, there were no Muslims in the HVO as of this point in time, August of 1993, because they had all been arrested and disarmed pursuant to orders issued by your predecessor, General Petkovic; true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were much fewer Muslims in the HVO after the betrayal on the 30th of June or earlier on when they were preparing for this, and that's correct, but it's not cause. This was the HVO's intention; it was because of the betrayal of the plan of the 30th of June. The Muslims and the HVO -- not all of them, but many of them attacked the HVO from the rear. They disarmed them and took over territory that they had, up until that point in time, been defending jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, the next section in this training programme is entitled "Serviceman in the HZ-HB Armed Forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. General Praljak, the Prosecutor has emphasised the issue of religion, the influence that the Catholic Church exercised, and we can see in the list, at page 18 in the English version, the role of someone called Alojzije Stepinac. As you are well aware, he was a cardinal in Zagreb, he was declared a martyr by the Pope, but in 1946 the Yugoslav authorities convicted him for having collaborated with the Ustasha. This is a well-known public fact. So having referred to him in a document intended for use by soldiers who, a priori, have no particular confession, even if most of them were Catholic, well, the fact that this was done, doesn't it mean that a signal is being given? Why is this reference made to the cardinal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For his moral position, Judge Antonetti. Naturally, I know about the work and the life of Cardinal Alojzije Stepinac, I know a lot about that. His stance in the course of the Second World War, his stance after the Second World War, his stance at trial -- well, later he was poisoned in prison, and he died as a result of this poisoning, but his guardian in prison, the guardian of all those prisons at the time the cardinal was there, well, it was Mr. Manolic, who has testified here. So he was beatified. And because of his moral position expressed in court in relation to all other counts, and he stated that his conscience was clear, and I'll repeat this before this Court, although naturally I can't compare myself with the cardinal, well, because of this position this is the reason for which we -- or, rather, I wanted to make a reference to this moral position. And under item 7, it says you have to be dedicated to order, you have to have a moral position, you have to opt for freedom, peace, and democracy for the future, and so on and so forth. This is a text that I stand by fully. There was absolutely nothing that would be tantamount to religious indoctrination here. As you can see from the list of literature, most of the authors are professors who published books of various political kinds. Dusan Bilandzic, for example, is included, who was a Communist. Bilandzic's book couldn't be a book referred to in the HVO as he was a Communist ideologue, and if there had been indoctrination in the HVO, we couldn't have referred to that book. I won't go into other details now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I have understood you correctly, in your opinion he represented moral authority. The Prosecution pointed this out to you, but he didn't insist on the fact. We can also see that you referred to the role of other religions; the Bogomils, Islam, the Orthodox religion. To your knowledge, who instructed the soldiers with regard to the existence of these other religions? Did you have any imams visiting? Did you have any Orthodox priests to instruct them, to provide them with explanations? Who provided them with lessons with regard to these other religions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professors of history instructed them about everything. There were no professors from churches, not from a single church. The people who instructed them were all laymen. They had an academic background. They were professors of history, and they addressed these issues, they instructed them. But, Your Honours, when a subject is discussed, and this is the case in all countries -- when you discuss French history, well, then it has to do with the history of the relationship with the Germans and the Spanish, and so on and so forth. It's not necessary to say, We're going to study French history and Spanish history. You study about French history and then you also study about the relationships that France had with other countries, naturally. And the Catholic Church, or the church in general up until the creation of modern states, played one of the most important roles in the history of all states. This is something that one can't avoid. It's not a matter of indoctrination. This was particularly the case in peoples who were not independent. Sometimes this was the only stronghold for preserving culture and language of a certain people in a certain territory. So this is what was studied. There were priests -- no priests of any kind who provided instruction at the seminars that we organised or at military academies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just go one step further. You have said that the Church, the Church, in general played one of the most important roles in the history of all states. I would like you to explain to the Chamber what importance they played for the Bosnians and for the Serbs. What you say is convincing for the Croats, but how about the Bosnians and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation was the same, Judge Trechsel. However we look at the situation, Ottoman's conquest that extended to the west up until -- as far as Vienna, well, the Muslims, as a religion, came into existence as a result of this conquest, they were converted, and this went on for centuries. The last cases were in the 19th century. I can provide you with evidence of this. So conversions in Mostar and Dreznica, according to our sources, took place in the 19th century. After the famous Battle of Kosovo, when the Turks defeated the Serbs, many Serbs moved out of that area and moved to Hungary. This was under the Carnojevici. They moved as far as Hungarian territory. They moved in the direction of the west, people sort of fleeing more and more towards the west for three centuries. There was constant movement of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm trying to stop you because you're going in a direction which I do not find is answering my question. Is it your point that what you have told us now, the conversion to Islam and what happened to the Serbs, that this is the work mainly of the Catholic Church, which you say has a paramount importance in history of all states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Judge Trechsel, I can't explain four centuries of history in three sentences, no matter what I do. The conversion was carried out by the Osmanlijas, not the Turks, the Osmanlijas, and this was done by taking the children to the "janjicari."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're not answering my question, and I take that as a fact. And please, Mr. Stringer, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I don't know what your question is. The Catholic Church didn't convert them. The Osmanlijas did, whether it concerned the Orthodox or the Catholic people, and this is how the Muslims came into existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, through conversion. So the people who came from Istanbul carried out administrative functions. When this empire fell, they returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This does not in any way contribute to the tasks of the Chamber. Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I actually want to come back to something you said in response to one of the questions from Judge Antonetti. In terms of the role of the church, you said sometimes this was the only stronghold for preserving culture and language of a certain people in a certain territory, so this is what was studied. This the top of page 11 of today's transcript. So, General, my question is: You've talked about the role that the church played, the Catholic Church, in preserving culture and language. I'm assuming your reference is to the Croatian people. Your view of the HVO, and I'm putting it to you it's quite evident from these texts we've been going over, is that the HVO was -- also intended to play a role -- the same role that the armed forces had to play a role in preserving Croatian culture and language in these Croatian territories and lands that are referred to in your training programme; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not a tribe down there for the HVO to protect the Croatian language. I even consider your question slightly insulting, but I have to answer the question because I have to do that. We are a people that have its own language. I'm talking about history, a difficult history, a centuries-old history, and we have to discuss it within a time-limit of three or four minutes, questions that it is very difficult to explain in such a short period of time. The HVO and the Croats had their own language, and it was called "Croatian."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase the question, and I know this is a delicate or it can be a delicate subject. We've talked a great deal, not just you but others as well, about the changing demographics, the reduction in the percentage of Croatian people living throughout various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You've also told us about your objective, the objective to establish an autonomous Croatian area in an area where Croat people would have the majority. So with those two factors in mind, General, can we agree that your HVO -- your vision of the HVO was that it would be an armed force intended to protect and to solidify this Croatian autonomous area you talk about as a means of preserving Croatian language and culture in the territories falling within the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political option changed from the Cutileiro plan onwards, and it was mostly proposed by the international community, in discussions that I need not refer to because we've discussed them at length already. I do not see what we were -- intended to defend when it's something that we own. We possess this. As a people, we belong to a certain civilisational circle, we speak a language, and the Croats call their language "Croatian," like any other nation. So I simply don't know what to say, except that I disagree with your theses because they're incorrect. I don't know what I could say in answer to your question, because the questions are put in such a way as if it was a crime to belong to a certain nation, to fight for the freedom of a certain state, and all the peoples who lived in these parts where the Croats formed a defensive force for themselves and others in the absence of any other possibility, be it international or the authority in Sarajevo, which began to develop other options and, of course, the Serb policies. So in view of such a situation, the HVO did the only possible thing that was right to do. It fought against aggression, it preserved Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, General. I'm going to move on briefly to the next section of this, this "Serviceman in the HZ-HB" section. This is the bottom of page 22 of the English. And, General, if you would turn -- actually, I'm going to skip across to pages 23 and 24, which in your version, General, is the ERN stamped -- ending with 0843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the religious issue, because together with my colleagues, we're endeavouring to understand the importance of religion. As you know, as your lawyers must have told you, that when the Chamber went to the hill of Hum, where we see the large cross above Mostar, and we were there with your counsel, the counsel who are here present, and from this position we looked at Mostar. Being there on the spot, I want to ask you: What could have been the impact of this cross on the mentality of the Muslims of Mostar, who saw clearly this cross? How could you explain to us the balance that might have existed between the various confessions and particularly through a document such as this one that you signed? How could one achieve an equilibrium among all those religions? And, briefly, this document, does it go in the direction of such an equilibrium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cross on the Hum hill was built after the war, Your Honour, just as many religious facilities were destroyed during the war. As far as I know, there are thousands of facilities of the Croatian Church that have been either destroyed or seriously damaged during the war. I have provided the documents to support this, and this can all be verified. I do not see any reason why a cross would bother anyone, just as at least 20 new mosques that have been built in Mostar should bother anyone. I think after the war, there were 20 new mosques built in Mostar. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are hundreds, of course, with the generous assistance of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and others, and this is reported on in the media. But if now we were to discuss this, an Orthodox Church is being built in Mostar on a hill facing Hum. If we were to start counting in this way, I don't think it would lead us anywhere. There are three confessions there. Each of them have their own temples. And to discuss whether the construction of a cross would bother the Muslims or the construction of a mosque bother the Christians, then there would be nothing left of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for the topics discussed here, and I repeat, they are absolutely free of any indoctrination. This is a purely historical review of things by lay professors, written in books. There's nothing bad in them. And, I repeat once again, I would sign this once again today, in fact, with pride because it is all absolutely clean, with emphasis on morality, honesty, ethical positions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we don't need to go back to the document, but I'm going to recall P01788. That was the document that we looked at earlier that you -- that had the minutes of the briefing in Central Bosnia, the handwritten minutes, that you and Mr. Coric and others were present at. In that document, you said - and I'm obviously paraphrasing because I don't have it in front of me - what you said was something like this: This is how it's going to be. We're going to fence off what is ours, and people that don't like it can leave. And we're seeing that same mentality in this document when you're talking about your vision of the HVO, General. The fact is that you had no interest in achieving any sort of equilibrium, as President Antonetti has raised the word. There's no equilibrium here in this training document. There's no intention of trying to accommodate the fact that different cultures, different religions and ethnic groups could perhaps wish to participate in the defence of these Croatian Community areas; isn't that true? The whole intention behind the HVO, your vision, is to not have equilibrium and to have only one orientation toward the Croat Catholic; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, it is not true. You've been asking me for five times now. Will you show me where this is stated? That is not correct. You cannot tell the American Army, in the Second World War, that, Let us study the greatness of Beethoven, Mozart and so on. What they study is the American history, and the enemy is described with very derogatory terms. You don't want me to quote those terms. We are an absolutely civilised army, as far as that is concerned. You should have read, in France -- or Hemingway's reports or thoughts about the Germans after the Second World War. What are we talking about? This is a war. There's no propaganda here. This is an absolutely civilised text, compared to other nations in a similar situation. And what you said that I said, no, it is somebody who wrote down that I said this, and he is hardly literate, and certainly he cannot convey my thoughts which have a certain subtlety which it is impossible to convey even now, never mind then. That is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I put the Prosecution case to you on this document, and I don't think that there's much point in us discussing that part of it anymore. What I want to do is to quickly move to the next section --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- which on -- beginning on the bottom of page 23 and then continuing the top of page 24 of the English is the curriculum on the serviceman in the HVO, and, General, this would appear to be basic training of soldiers on various ways to conduct themselves as soldiers. We see topics on basic rights and duties of HVO soldiers; order and internal service; relations within the HVO Army; military discipline. And it moves down. Criminal acts against the armed forces. And we can look at some of these topics, General, but I'm going to put it to you that: Would you agree with me that, at least in this section, there's no reference -- there's no separate training in respect of the laws of armed conflict; isn't that true? And, in fact, I'm going to put it to you that the whole training programme does not address the issue of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Among the duties of members of the HVO and the moral responsibility of the members of the HVO, therefore, item 1, 6, 7, criminal offences against the armed forces, not against the armed forces of the HVO, but against any armed forces. In each of these sections and at special seminars, each serviceman was instructed on the basics of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is that nothing in this training manual explicitly relates to training in the law of war. There are references here to any number of things, such as criminal acts against the armed forces, which could just as equally include something like refusal to mobilise or misconduct by taking your gun into town when you're not allowed to. So, again, there's nothing overtly in this document about training in the law of war; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. The basic rights and duties of HVO members refer to what you have just said; that is, carrying weapons, et cetera. Whereas, criminal acts against armed forces doesn't mean going around town armed. It is something quite different. And the fact that this is explicitly not mentioned, there are broader issues. Moral responsibility is broader than criminal responsibility under international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So are you telling us, General, that training that your conscripts received in terms of the law of war was more broad, and that it was not specifically targeting the various issues related to armed conflict or the Law of Armed Conflict? I mean, you talk about morality, which I suppose could include not burning down civilians' homes when they're not legitimate military targets, but I don't see anything explicitly in here about these sorts of specific humanitarian law issues. You just tell them to be moral, and does that cover it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat, sir, that within the framework of these issues there were discussions also about the law of war; not either/or, but including it. A smaller group is included within a broader group of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if it is not specifically stated in the way you believe it should be stated, you reach the conclusion that it was not mentioned, and this simply is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And earlier on, this is -- this is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking now at page 28 of the English, which is the next topic you'll find in your programme, which is on the trainee. I'm on page 0845 of your version, "Trainee." And on page 28, there's a box that contains all those relevant topics, and again these are basic training issues for new soldiers, and we would not appear to be finding any training in this section on the Law of Armed Conflict. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is quite a separate section, how a unit operates. And when you're teaching someone how to salute and what position he should take in the line-up, or how to dig trenches, you can't, in such a section, discuss those other topics, because these are separate issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. I accept that. I'm just trying to clarify where, in this programme, international humanitarian law would or would not have been addressed. I mean, it's clear that new soldiers have to be taught a lot of other things as well. Now, we have another section here on infantry weapons and target practice, and again this is page 30-31 of the English. These are clearly legitimate areas -- necessary areas for training, General, but would you agree that international humanitarian law would not have been dealt with in this section either?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. If someone is being taught how to shoot, and while he's undergoing training in those days, and in that situation humanitarian war is not discussed. You can talk about it before that or after that, in a conference hall, or wherever such a topic is being discussed. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then let's turn now to page 38 of the English, page 0850 of the original language version, General. And here we've got a listing of training sessions on what's called tactical training, and all the topics are laid out there; 29 topics, actually. And we could look at all of these, but I'm not going to do that. One that caught my attention, I thought that might have some relevance for us, is item number 22, "Combat in Settled Areas," because clearly combat in settled areas would raise issues linked to humanitarian international law. So let's take a look at that one, which is on page 58 of the English, and this is page 0858 of your text, General, topic number 22, "Combat in Settled Areas." And, again, it's training on marching into settled areas, characteristics of combat in settled areas, moving up to buildings, position inside buildings, et cetera. So there's no reference to civilians in here, General, and there's no reference to measures that are required under international law to be taken when you have civilians present in areas where combat is or might be taking place. Isn't that true, no reference to international humanitarian law here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. This is teaching a soldier how to take control of a building from which the fire is coming. This is a tactical part of training. It is identical to an American army. When there's tactical training, then there's no mention about moral dilemmas in an inhabited area. Nowhere has it been settled well, even in the doctrine of the American Army, because everything is very vague. It is important to capture the building from which fire is coming without hurting civilians, and yet we see collateral damage with an unbelievable number of civilian casualties, and I believe everyone in this courtroom is aware of that as well as I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, of course we're aware of that, General, and we're aware that these are legitimate training issues. My point is that the very complex issues related to international humanitarian law, when you're fighting in settled areas, do not appear -- can we agree that they are not dealt with in this particular part of the programme?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot agree, because this is a tactical section and in another area, at a different time, the same people would study about the things you're referring to, behaviour on the ground. And I've told you a dozen times, as far as the HVO in Mostar was concerned while I was there, regarding the legitimacy of its objectives, it behaved in an absolutely civilised manner, far above the standard set by international humanitarian law in that respect, and in the positive sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think I got my answer, then, is what you've just indicated to us is that training on the international humanitarian law aspects took place in another area at a different time. Are you telling us that there was separate training on that that you're referring to that is not contained in this training programme we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are contained in this part of the training, I have mentioned that, but not at the time when soldiers are undergoing tactical training, when they're being taught how to fire, how to cover another soldier. This is tactical training that every soldier is exposed to, and while he's doing that, it's only tactical training. And while I was there, you saw the proposal of the Red Cross when the war was at its peak. We conducted additional seminars about these things contained in international humanitarian law and the Law of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You recall, General, Andrew Pringle, who came and testified as an expert witness in this trial?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P09549, which must be the first exhibit in the next binder. And, General, I'd like to direct you to paragraph 47 of General Pringle's report, which in your version, the Croatian version, is page 20; page 13 of the original English. And this is what General Pringle says in paragraph 47. I don't think the first part of it is very controversial. He says: "Soldiers, and especially if conflict is imminent or under way, should therefore be trained in how to treat civilians and prisoners of war, and their obligations under the Laws of Armed Conflict. This was indeed recognised in the HVO as can be seen from the training programme for soldiers. Training requirements included 'soldier as prisoner of war,' 'attitude towards prisoner of war, searching prisoners,' 'capturing enemy soldiers/officers, treatment of prisoners,' 'capturing and imprisoning the enemy.' Whilst compliance with the Geneva Conventions and International Laws of War was mandated at the highest levels of the HZ-HB," and we know he's referring here now in the footnote to the Decree on Armed Forces, General Pringle says: "I have noticed no reference in the documents I have been given by the Office of the Prosecutor that refer to the requirement to train soldiers in their legal obligations and responsibilities under the International Laws of War." He says -- he continues by saying: "The 1988 JNA Regulations on this subject are thorough and comprehensive and could have provided the proper basis for such training." Now, General, we see just in the previous footnote, 4142, one of the documents that he had at hand when he wrote his report is this very training programme that we've just been going over, and General Pringle, after reviewing it, concluded that he didn't see requirements to train soldiers in their legal obligations and responsibilities under the International Laws of War. So would you agree with me, General, that, in fact, if there were such requirements for training, they are to be found elsewhere? If anywhere at all, they're not contained in your programme that we've been going over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to react to this question put by Mr. Stringer because the document that we have just been looking at, which Mr. Stringer didn't show to General Praljak -- or, rather, the item, item 21, wasn't shown to General Praljak, where it refers to treating prisoners. It concerns searching the terrain and fighting in forests, how to deal with those arrested, wounded, and killed. So if the general is being shown the report drafted by the Expert Witness Pringle, and if such question is being put, then it would be fair to show the general item 21, which states that they were trained about how to deal with prisoners, those arrested, and those who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to add that in item 24 of the document that we have been analysing, reference is made to capturing enemy officers, and further on in the document this subject is dealt with. So the Petkovic Defence would like to make this objection too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Let me Mr. Stringer respond to the objections. Mr. Stringer, it would appear that according to Defence counsel, the document does explicitly refer to the way in which prisoners should be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can respond, Mr. President. I noticed that one of the accused was indicating he wanted to say something, and I don't know whether General Petkovic wants to speak or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreter cannot hear General Petkovic. The interpreter still cannot hear General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that General Praljak forgot about how some soldiers were trained. The title of the document is "Basic Training." Ask General Praljak whether this is followed by specialist training and more time is spent on this training, and then finally is common training provided? We have three forms of training. We just have the first, initial document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one asks me about this. How am I to answer if a question isn't put to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, General Petkovic has said, and I must say that I hadn't realised this, that in fact this document amounts to basic training, which does not exclude the possibility of there being more specialised forms of training in certain domains. So were there other forms of training, and in fact this document is only a narrow part of the training provided because there are other forms of training provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a restricted part, but not narrow. It's part of the training provided. There are two other forms of training provided. You've heard about that. Your Honours, General Pringle examined the documents provided to him by the Prosecution. I brought some documents here that had to do with the continuous, incessant training with regard to the Law of War. The books on the Law of War are very big. There were parts that dealt with maritime war, positions of countries, and so on, so we couldn't deal with everything. We dealt with the parts that might have to do with the situations the HVO soldiers would be confronted with; for example, how to treat arrested people, wounded individuals, how to behave in the course of combat, what soldiers' duties were. So there are many books -- thousands of books that were distributed to everyone who was trained at the end of that training, and even if someone didn't go and have training, they were provided with such books. This was a daily theme that was dealt with whenever we had half an hour to spare. So we would extract certain sections and then we would say, If such and such a case, well, then, such and such is the case. No, Your Honour, there were various forms of training. There was basic training, specialist training, the final training that was provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to General Petkovic, there were other forms of training that were provided, and there are certain subjects, topics, that you don't see in the document, International Humanitarian Law, that might have been referred to in the course of other forms of training provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, International Humanitarian Law is dealt with in this document too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So everyone has understood the matter. Yes, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise. I rose earlier on. I believe that the basic problem is the result of the following: I was having a look at the English version that refers to paragraph 47. This concerns the Pringle report, and I can see that the English version is identical to the Croatian version, but in the English version I can see a certain sentence after the one that the Prosecution read out. That's the first sentence in which the following is stated: "Soldiers, especially when faced with an imminent conflict, have to be trained with regard to how to treat civilians and prisoners of war, and they have to be informed of their duties in accordance with the Laws and Customs of War." In the following sentence, the expert, Pringle, says the HVO really recognised this fact, as can be seen from the training programme for soldiers. Reference is made to footnote 34 then, which contains Exhibit 04142, and this is the training programme that we were examining before this document, and then it continues. Training requirements included: soldier as prisoner of war; attitude towards prisoners of war; searching prisoners; capturing enemy soldiers/officers; treatment of prisoners. And then what follows is not important at this point in time. I would just like to say that what I have just read out, what Mr. Pringle says in item 47, is contradictory, because if he first talks about this and then refers to footnote 34 and says that he found a reference to the Geneva Conventions, and it says he didn't have this at his disposal, well, if that is the case I think there's a problem with this report and not with General Praljak at this point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The text says what it says. I read it differently. We can -- we can read the Pringle report and his conclusion that after referring to the documents, that he doesn't find a reference in the documents to the requirement to train soldiers in their legal obligations and responsibilities. And if you look at General Praljak's training programme, Mr. President, and I was just getting ready to put this to him, he's talked about tactical training and what to do in tactical situations where there's no real emphasis on Humanitarian International Law, but in fact were we do not have in this entire document is any specific, independent reference to training in International Humanitarian Law. It's simply a side issue or it's part of some tactical training which, Oh, by the way, if you're fighting in combat areas, this is how to move around inside the buildings. So we all have the documents, and we can draw our own conclusions from them, Mr. President, but that's -- that's simply the Prosecution case that's being put here. The general said there was other training as well, and the Trial Chamber may be -- may accept that testimony or it may consider that in light of other evidence, but our view is simply that, as I put it to the general, there is not a sufficient -- indeed, there's only, at best, oblique reference to it in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, the Judges will arrive at their own conclusions, but an additional point. In 1992-1993, we know that the international community was present in the field, we've seen this in numerous documents, so that all these conflicts were unfolding before the eyes of foreigners. And given such a situation, the command structure that you represented, as of the 27th of July, 1993, shouldn't the Command explain to the soldiers that it was necessary to pay attention because collateral damage, a mistake, et cetera, could be amplified by the international community, and that's why it was necessary to respect international conventions and to be particularly cautious when it comes to the Law of War? So were such things said to your soldiers? Because it is true that Mr. Pringle's report states that he hadn't seen a document that we've examined, any references made to the subject, but it's not categorically stated because he referred to the JNA document of 1988 with regard to that subject. So it's understood that all this must have been explained to the soldiers. I don't know anything. I'm not an HVO soldier, so I can't say. But I'm wondering whether you, yourself, and your officers, the officers who surrounded you, I'm wondering whether you and your officers told the soldiers to be careful, because there was the Spanish Battalion, the British Battalion, there was the European Mission, the international press was present as well, and all this would be carefully scrutinised, so did you and your officers intervene, regardless of the document that is incomplete, to tell them that they should be careful, and to say that there are certain texts, laws, rules of conduct, and if any mistakes are made, the consequences could be quite negative for the HVO? Is this something that they were told by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in that way. I never told them, Don't commit mistakes because the Spanish or French Battalion are there. I wasn't interested in that. I told them about honour, honesty, moral responsibility, the Law of War, because as individuals these are things that they should not have done, and not because a journalist was present who might draft a report on the subject. That wasn't our position. Anyone could have been there or no one. That wasn't my moral basis for what I instructed them in. I have provided you with documents from the Croatian Army, documents in which I draft and explain laws, and I say, You won't be granted an amnesty because you are Croatian soldiers, you'll be punished even more severely because of that. I told them how severe the punishment would be, and for what. And I said it wasn't because the Americans were there. I wasn't interested in that. I said they would be punished because they were men, they were soldiers, and these were things that should not be done. And that was done systematically, in continual ways, and I did this on a daily basis. And when we discuss these documents about honesty and so on and so forth, well, this goes beyond what International Law prescribes. So to tell them what the Law of War in maritime cases [indiscernible], that's absurd. We dealt with what they might be confronted with. We didn't have to instruct them about how to conduct themselves if a dam was broken, or we didn't tell them whether a certain commander could take a decision if it was a decision that could be taken internationally but not nationally. We didn't have time for that. But we instructed them with regard to what was necessary. They knew everything, not because the French were present but because this is how they had to fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, if I could ask you to turn to page 15 of your version of the Pringle report. I'm going to direct you to some of his text contained in paragraphs 38 and 39. Here, General Pringle is talking about command climate, and in paragraph 38 he says: "A commander, by force of his personality, leadership, command style, and general behaviour, has a considerable influence on the morale, sense of direction, and performance of his staff and subordinate commanders. Any commander of any nationality will influence his staff and subordinate commanders for good or evil. Command climate is as relevant to senior commanders as it is to more junior commanders. Plainly, the more senior the commander, the wider the influence of his personal command climate. Senior commanders set the tone for their commands. Command climate is a subject often discussed in military doctrinal manuals in order to encourage commanders to reflect on the implications of getting the command climate right." And then he continues in the next paragraph to -- he cites some of the text from your own report -- excuse me, your own programme, P04142 that we've been talking about today, where he quotes -- and this is actually from page 69 of the English version of your report, General, page 0864 of the Croatian version, the original version, where your -- your training programme says: "A good and capable commander is characterised by knowledge, both tactical and technical, and an ability for exemplary command. The commander, the way he communicates with men, his appearance, and conduct influence the creation of the image in the minds of the unit's members that he is a reliable and capable commander." Now, General, I want to use that to talk about your conduct, the command climate that you set in your dealings and your communications with your subordinates. If you would turn first, please, to Exhibit P01162. Now, this is from the 16th of January, 1993, General, and we're going to talk about Gornji Vakuf in more detail probably later this week. This is a report of Colonel Siljeg, commander of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone, sending this report to the Main Staff and also to the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone. And as we all know, at 2000 hours on the 16th of January, 1993, the situation in Gornji Vakuf was quite tense. General, if I recall from your testimony, you arrived in this area -- it may not have been Gornji Vakuf itself, you may have been in Prozor, but you arrived in this area, I believe, either on the evening of the 15th or the 16th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the evening between the 15th and 16th, or perhaps the morning of the 16th of January in Prozor -- in Rama, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So you were in Rama. And so that on the 16th of January, at 2000 hours, at 8.00 in the evening, then, you were in Rama, you were in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were in communication with Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in contact with him, partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was he also in Prozor, in Rama, or was he at a different location?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. Naturally, he was constantly travelling between Rama, Uskoplje, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf. I mean, he attended discussions up there with the ABiH, and this was mostly with the presence of the English part of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, General, coming back to the previous text from General Pringle's report and your own programme, in terms of command climate, I think it's useful again for us to recall what your position was, what your -- the various positions you held at the time that you arrived in Prozor on the 16th of January, 1993. Now, General, at that time it's correct, is it not, that you were an assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were also a member of the VONS, what we call the VONS, which was the Security and Defence Council of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were a major general of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You arrived in Gornji Vakuf, having been sent there or asked by President Tudjman to go there in order to calm the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic asked me to go and try and solve the situation, the conflict, the conflict that had started a few days earlier, the 11th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this document, Colonel Siljeg's report, actually makes a reference to what you've just indicated, negotiations or talks that were taking place between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Looking at the bottom of page 2 of the English, where he reports that that evening, the 16th, he and Colonel Andric negotiated with BH Army representatives, no results. He says: "Unless there is an agreement, Gornji Vakuf southern strongholds will be taken and our line strengthened." Do you see that, General? This is the second-to-last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, could you just read out for us then the next sentence, which is the last paragraph of this report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading as follows: "General Praljak informed them that they would be overthrown if they did not cease with their actions and if they did not accept the decisions taken by the HZ-HB government." They would be annihilated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We're talking about command climate, and so I think it's important to be very precise about the language that we're referring to here. And in fairness to you, I want to make sure that we're fairly attributing language to you or that the interpretation is one that is fair. General, we've been given the word "annihilated." It was -- initially, we were told -- I guess this is for the benefit of all, not you, since you're listening in a different language. Your message is that they would be overthrown, and then the interpreter indicated or gave us the word "annihilated." Now, General, this is a message that you directed to the representatives of the BH Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, when it says here that General Praljak sent them a message, I assume that means that General Praljak sent a message to the representatives of the BH Army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Praljak spoke with Siljeg, and Siljeg certainly added something that I didn't say. In military terms, it says, You'll be trampled over or overthrown. It can mean many things, and naturally it has nothing to do with the civilian part of life. But this word, "trample over," "overthrow," has nothing to do with the logic followed up there, and that can be seen from the previous passage that you read out. If the negotiations are fruitless, then only the southern strongholds around the town will be taken, strongholds established by the ABiH for a while, and our lines on Podovi will be strengthened. So those will be the results if no agreement is reached. And then he said, You'll be overthrown or, You'll be trampled over. That's not true. The HVO just had to carry out an active defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've got to answer my questions. I can't let you just go on and on. What you've just told us, then, is that whatever the message was that is attributed to you, you gave a message to Siljeg, and Siljeg then passed that message on to the BH Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I spoke with Siljeg, and we wanted to see how we could put an end to the operation that had already been launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to insist on precision here. Now, it says here that you sent a message. Is Siljeg telling us the truth there? Is there a message from you that went across to the BH Army or was there not? Is this report just false?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, the report isn't precise. Naturally, I spoke to Siljeg and Andric when they went to attend discussions earlier on when I was up there in November. It's quite simple. I discussed the matter with them and have them move from positions as a result of which the HVO is in an impossible situation. I told Siljeg to tell them to move from those positions, to tell them that we should reach an agreement so that an end was put to the operation. That's all that was said, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in order to save time, I think that perhaps there is something that is not fully understood in the Siljeg report. Well, it's the 16th of January, 1993, that's the date, and at the time there are allegations, the ultimatum of the 15th of January, and then I can see a sentence, apart from the term "our forces." It says "our forces," and then Colonel Siljeg explains the following. He says, We are starting with more intensive operations, with regard to enemy movement, and the regrouping of ABiH forces. In military terms, when I read this part - and if I'm mistaken, you'll tell me - but I have the impression that Colonel Siljeg, realising that the ABiH, the enemy, is engaged in movement in regrouping its forces, believes that it is necessary to intervene, and in this case you would have sent a message according to which if they didn't accept the decisions of the HZ-HB, it would be necessary to annihilate them, crush them, I don't know what. Apparently, there's a translation problem there. So given this scenario or according to this document -- I don't know whether it's true or not, but according to this scenario, first of all, the ABiH that is moving and regrouping -- you have the ABiH moving and regrouping, and the HVO intervenes, and you take action, you send a message referred to by Colonel Siljeg. So in military terms, do things unfold as described by Colonel Siljeg? Is it the ABiH that was engaged in movement and you then intervened, or was the situation the reverse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I have to say yet again that having spent so much time on determining the facts about the matter, we spent a lot of time on showing that the ABiH was digging in in all the dominant hills around Gornji Vakuf. That started several months earlier, and positions that we held with the ABiH -- together with the ABiH, were 20 kilometres away from Raduski Kamen. I have to repeat that for months, and especially in December, at my request, on my initiative, Andric and Siljeg were involved in a series of discussions with the ABiH to ensure that they would move these strongholds. And we've seen photographs of these strongholds. We've seen this with the English officer from a certain battalion. We saw the positions on the hills around the town and in town that they had occupied. I also said that the so-called ultimatum was agreed with Alija Izetbegovic. I took it to Mostar on the 15th because Izetbegovic authorised it. It was necessary to take action, but later he changed his mind. I went up there to deal with the matter. I couldn't put an end to this, and I didn't want to put an end to the HVO defence, to the HVO attempt to move the ABiH or dislodge the ABiH from the positions they were holding, because given the positions they held, they would have been able to kill the HVO as required. I then got in touch with Petkovic and others who were in Geneva. There was a cease-fire that was agreed on. And we prevented entry into Gornji Vakuf, and things calmed down after a while. So that is the background to this history. So to be crushed, in military terms, means you'll lose. To be crushed, overthrown, or annihilated, well, I don't use such terms. But Mr. Siljeg, who is a soldier, used such terms; we'll overthrow, annihilate them, this is something he added. But it's a fact that the ABiH launched an operation, they sent a brigade towards Prozor. There are scores of documents about this entire situation that we have examined here. But in the previous item, what is the objective of the HVO? Well, if they won't fight with us against the Serbs, then we have to take the southern strongholds around the town, the strongholds held by the ABiH. What do they want such strongholds for if we are a joint force? They had interrupted the communications towards Central Bosnia, they had taken up these strongholds, and in the evening the conflict was ended, although they were defeated in military terms. Well, no entry was made into Gornji Vakuf, no attempt was made at the conquest. I managed to halt these young men, they trusted me. And that's my style, if you're talking about a commander's style. And it's true that the general has a right to address such matters. There is a command climate, and you have hundreds of documents on how I commanded and how I treated everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll stop there. You have answered the question at length. Mr. Stringer will certainly return to the subject after the break, because it's time to have our break. So we will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, at the time of the break, we were looking at P01162, and I'm just going -- well, first, before I come back to this exhibit, I want to get one clarification. You indicated, and I know you've said this before, there is a reference to a decision there, a decision of the HZ-HB, and I believe your testimony, General, is that at some time on the 15th of January, you had a meeting with Alija Izetbegovic in which he agreed to, essentially, the text of the decision or the -- what we're calling -- the Prosecution's calling the ultimatum on resubordination. Do you understand which meeting I'm referring to, your meeting with Alija Izetbegovic on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Mr. Izetbegovic did not agree with that decision, but that decision was drafted together with Mr. Izetbegovic and some of his men, together with his defence minister, Mr. Bozo Rajic, and I think this was on the 13th and the 14th. These talks went on for two days, I believe; not all day, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where did those talks take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the Esplanade hotel, I think that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Which city is that in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you've said Alija Izetbegovic was present, as well as Mr. Bozo Rajic and other people who were with Mr. Izetbegovic. Who was present on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that I participated in a part of the talks and Gojko Susak in another part, so I can't know -- tell you exactly in which part which wording was proposed, by who. In the host of meetings that were held, it's difficult to say, but I'm almost quite certain that it was at the Esplanade Hotel in Zagreb. Whether somewhere else as well, I can't remember each and every name regarding the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So these meetings took place during the 13th and 14th of January, and you were present at some but not all of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. To the best of my recollection, the 14th, I'm sure of. Whether something was started on the 13th, in the evening, I don't know. I do remember the 14th, and the 15th in the morning, I remember, when I went to see Mr. Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman at the Presidential Palace in Zagreb. The text was ready, it was agreed and approved, and it was to be announced. The defence minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the government, Bozo Rajic, was due to announce it. And I took it with me to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When did you leave Zagreb to go to Mostar, at what time of day, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before noon, whether it was 11.00 or 10.00. In any event, I think it was before noon or around that time. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you would have arrived in Mostar at what time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, in the evening. It gets dark quite early. What the time was, how long the trip took, I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So at some point -- and when you left -- when you left Zagreb, when you left Zagreb at 11.00 or 10.00 in the morning on the 15th, then you had with you this text that you say was agreed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was carrying it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did the text have signatures on it? Did people actually sign off on all this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They agreed with the text. It was just Mr. Bozo Rajic who was due to sign the text. It was concluded and approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who signed the text on the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that anyone signed it on behalf of the Bosnian Muslims. I just said that it was agreed upon in its entirety, and it was Bozo Rajic who was due to announce it and sign it, at least he was due to be the first one, and then it would follow in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So your evidence is that this was an oral agreement on the text?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the end, everyone agreed with the text. Or, rather, I know that Mr. Izetbegovic agreed with it. I know that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were present when he agreed to that text?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the Esplanade. This was on the 14th, when the talks were finished and when it was said, Okay, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll come back to this when we talk more about Gornji Vakuf. General, I want to come back to the document we've been looking at, P01162, and I'm simply going to put it to you, General, because based on what you've said about it already, I don't think it's something that we can reach much agreement on, but I'm going to put the Prosecution case to you on this document. The fact is, General, that Colonel Siljeg accurately reported in this document, which he sent to the Main Staff, that you sent a message to the BH Army telling them that they would be crushed, or annihilated, or over-run if they did not accept the decisions of the HZ-HB; isn't that true, General? And that your message to them went out upon or after your arrival in Prozor-Rama on the 16th of January; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not in this form. It was not a question of accepting the decision, but that they should stop operations and withdraw from the lines. That was what it all boiled down to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the decision of the HZ-HB that's referred to here is, in fact, its decision in which it issued the ultimatum that we'll be talking about whereby the HZ-HB directed that ABiH units in Vance-Owen Cantons 3, 8, and 10 would have to subordinate themselves to the HVO; that's the decision that's being referred to here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision says what it says, and it was not an ultimatum. It was a joint agreement, the aim of which was to prevent this kind of possible conflict between the army and the HVO or, to be more precise, not conflicts, but repeated and continuous provocations by the BH Army, and they're considering that they were the only ones who were entitled to Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they were prevented from achieving this by the Chetniks and the Ustasha. When they needed weapons, we were fine, and when certain areas were to be taken, then we were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, bringing you back to the original issue, which is command climate, what's happening here is that we have someone who's just arrived from the highest levels within the Croatian Defence Ministry, is a general in the Croatian Army, he's among the inner circle of President Tudjman, and so the climate that's created when such a person tells the other side that they'll be annihilated or crushed if they don't accept a political decision of the HZ-HB, that's going to, in fact, create a climate in which the HVO is going to deal, in fact, swiftly and strongly to any failure on the part of the ABiH to accept the HZ-HB decisions; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, it is not. Firstly, because in hundreds of my documents you can see exactly how I write and what kind of climate I create. That's number 1. Secondly, this was not a decision by the HZ-HB, but it was a question of the BH Army ceasing aggressive actions against the HVO, and the climate was -- the climate that I created was the one when I managed, by force of authority, to carry out the command that came from Geneva, from General Petkovic and Mate Boban, and from Izetbegovic for the hostilities to cease. A climate was created because we did not take advantage of this situation to take control of Gornji Vakuf. The climate was created by the fact that the trenches were filled in that they had dug out, and we saw this from a number of documents, including those from the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you claimed, actually, that you were sent down to calm the situation. In fact, the climate that you created there by sending such a message here, that was clearly well known to and, in fact, conveyed by your subordinate, Colonel Siljeg, had the absolute opposite effect to calming the situation; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Siljeg did not accurately convey the words. He used this word "annihilation" or "crushing." It's a word used by soldiers. But what is true is that I agreed, until the order came to cease hostilities, that the deputy chief of Staff, Mr. Andric, and Mr. Siljeg - these are all one-star generals - that they do have the right to lead a military operation to liberate their forces from a total encirclement in the way as the Chetniks and the BH Army. Therefore, I don't agree with you and any interpretation that you are trying to enter into the transcript of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's look at another document to talk about, again, the command climate that's created by the things that you say and write. The next exhibit is P10936. Now, General, I know that you claim that part of this is a forgery or is not an authentic document, in that it does not contain your signature, and I'm going to refer you to -- we're not going to look at it, P2280. But P10936, General, is actually -- consists of three documents, all of which relate to the same order, your order, I'm putting it to you, in which you directed Colonel Siljeg in the North-Western Herzegovina Operations Zone to: "If they don't stop, you are free to act as you see fit. Pound them with artillery and with whatever else you can think of. Flatten everything in sight." Now, General, we see that in this document - we have it in different versions or different stages of preparation - first there's a handwritten document which is also 2280, which you claim is a forgery. We then see the same document in a subsequent draft form, bearing the stamp of the HVO Main Staff, on the 10th of May, 1993, under which is the handwritten word "Brada," which is a reference to you, I put it to you. And then, thirdly, we see the document in the form of an electronic packet communication over your name. It's a poor copy that was not completely translated because they were not able to do the entire translation, but it clearly again bearing the stamp of the HVO Main Staff, the same date, 10th of May, 1993, and the other references, such as the "Broj" number. The fact is, General, that this establishes, doesn't it, that you, in fact, did instruct or give Colonel Siljeg the green light, if you will, to flatten everything in sight; isn't that true? This is your order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at this Tribunal your colleague already asked me about this order, when I testified in the Martinovic case, Martinovic-Naletilic. I don't know what I should say to you. Anyone who glanced at my handwriting and who knows my orders -- this has nothing to do with me, neither the handwriting, nor the signature, nor the style, nor the method. By a simple analysis of anything -- you don't need any specialised analysis, an analysis of any of my letters would show that I have absolutely nothing to do with this. I'm not interested in finding out how this reached you. I don't care. This simply has nothing to do with me. Now, if you say that it has --
