utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've got more questions on this. I'm going to put it to you that, in fact, this is precisely how you talk, language like this, broad language, incendiary language. You've used it in the courtroom. I'm putting to you that, in fact, when it says "flatten everything in sight," that's precisely the way you talk and those were precisely the instructions that you conveyed to Colonel Siljeg; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all that I have said about these documents, I have no further comment in answer to your question. I will not comment on your question. They are, in my view, absurd, and I think perhaps it's not as simple as all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is showing you this document which, for him, is a document that supports his position, his thesis. You say, I've already answered, I have nothing more to say about it, et cetera. Very well. But in order to try and convince us that this is a false document, you need to provide certain evidence. It's not sufficient to say, I've already answered. We know that you have answered. But it is at the very heart of his position, because you have seen that Mr. Stringer works in a highly-professional manner and he is showing, by a whole series of arguments and documents, and within this series there is this document. Either you must explain that it is a false document because you see the reference number, the date, the 10th of May, Mostar, you can recall what I was doing [as interpreted], et cetera, Brada, yes, no, I have -- I'm not in the custom of signing in this way, and so on. But if you don't do that, what do we have in the transcript? You know that this is no secret. What do the Judges do? They look at the transcript, they look at the documents, and they look at what the accused or his counsel have said, and then they put away all this evidence and they reach a certain conclusion. That is how these things are done. Therefore, when you say, I've already answered, let us move on, it is your choice. Have you understood? This is an important document for the Prosecution. If you're challenging it, you must show to those who are judging you that these documents, they are a false document, that they came from here or there. I don't know what, but have you to provide some evidence. So I give the floor again to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General -- excuse me, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I recognise that the President's made some observations. I'm not finished with this one. I've got another document to show you that relates to this document. So my proposal, with the President's permission, is to go to the next document. We can round off the issue in its entirety, and then, General, you can make the comments that you want to make. General, the next exhibit is P09768 -- excuse me, 9769. This is dated the 10th of May, 1993. It's an urgent request for action from Commander Siljeg to the HVO Defence Department and to the HVO -- to the HZ-HB HVO Mostar. In the centre part - this is the part I want to direct you to - in all capital letters he's saying: "Give ABiH -- call ABiH and give them an ultimatum. Tell them that unless they stop the attack on Klis and Boksevica, I am going to use artillery to level Jablanica to the ground. "While they are quiet in Jablanica and we cannot fire at them, they are attacking us. I request an urgent answer." And this document bearing the stamp of the HVO Main Staff, 10th of May, 1993, at 2025 hours. What I want to direct your attention to, General, is in the upper left-hand corner, where you have the reference or the "Broj" number for this document, strictly confidential 01-432. Now, let's go back to the previous exhibit, P10936. P10936 is a reply to request strictly confidential 01-432, and it's in this document, General, that you tell Siljeg to: "Pound them with artillery and whatever else you can think of. Flatten everything in sight." Now, General, the fact is we know from looking at Siljeg's urgent request that your response is, in fact, a genuine, authentic HVO document in which you did use this language. You were referring specifically to Colonel Siljeg; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I have repeatedly -- in this case, when this document was shown, I have repeated and I will repeat again, it is not my handwriting on the first or second document. It is not my signature on the first or second document. It is not my style, either, because it would re-appear again in the documents that I did sign. I reached Mostar on the 11th of May, and I explained how much time I spent there, what happened when I left, and what I did after that, and I have no idea who, why, or how prepared this document, how it reached this file. I cannot provide any additional information in connection with it. But I have asked that this be sent for -- to a handwriting expert for an analysis to see whether I wrote this. They could compare it with my handwriting, though I in fact think that that is not necessary because this differs so much from my own handwriting. So I can say no more about this, except that this has nothing to do with me, the handwriting, the signature, the order, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, excuse me, but whether or not you physically wrote these words out yourself, they are your words. They're words that you dictated to someone else, perhaps. They're words that are made on your approval, and ultimately, going through the HVO Main Staff system, were communicated to Siljeg as part of a packet communication over your name. Isn't that true, whether or not you actually hand-wrote them yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would have at least signed them, Mr. Prosecutor. It is possible that someone may have written it, but I would have signed it. Where was I, furthermore, at the time? If you want -- in the host of forged documents that were provided to this Tribunal by various secret services, if you want to make me into something that I am not, it's up to you. This has nothing to do with me. I have nothing more to say about it, and it's up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that this document, P10936, the response to Siljeg, is an illegal order, in that it gives him the authorisation to use artillery without distinguishing between civilian and non-civilian or military targets? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the targets are not mentioned here. In such cases, when you're giving an order even on the ground, you can say, Destroy the trenches, or the bunkers, or something, but there's nothing here. Where, who should they attack, what should he attack, what should he destroy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I don't have the list of your witnesses in front of me, unfortunately. It seems to me that you did envisage at some point the arrival of Colonel Siljeg. If Siljeg were to testify, he would have explained to whom he addressed this document, for document P9769 is very clear. It asks for authority to use the artillery, because he has the intention of flattening Jablanica, so as the issue is beyond his competencies, he is addressing himself to the higher level. So I don't know whether Siljeg is coming or not. If he's not coming, he could have written a letter in response to your counsel, saying he was aware of this particular document, with the number, and he confirms by letter that his interlocutor was not General Praljak, the document being 1969. But the HVO commander was not you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Furthermore, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the Prosecutor had a lengthy conversation with Siljeg which consists of three or four binders. Siljeg doesn't know who gave him this order, he doesn't know that. And in this document, he's not addressing me, he doesn't say, Praljak, respond. He says -- I don't know what he says. He's addressing himself to the Main Staff. And as far as I know, when I got there on the 11th, Petkovic wasn't there because he was somewhere in Central Bosnia, so I don't know. If the Prosecutor had wanted to, he would have brought Siljeg to confirm his case. I keep having to prove my innocence. Let the Prosecutor prove that this is my document and my signature and that the document was addressed to me, Siljeg's letter. Why would I defend myself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we already know that it is up to the Prosecution to prove things. We all know that. We have a document that you are challenging, but now you have just said something. You said, Mr. Siljeg, and there are three or four binders of his interview as a witness or a suspect - I don't know, and you apparently say that he was asked questions. You know better than me about all those documents, because as you know, all the documents are not under the control of the Judges, so I don't know what Colonel Siljeg may have said. But what did Siljeg tell the Prosecutor when he was asked about this document? If you can remember, what did he say? Because if I had checked the documents, I would have the answer, but as I do not have control over all of the documents, you can tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let me interrupt you, both of you, because, as a matter of fact, since both of you speak very quickly and without a pause, that is why now there is no indication that the second paragraph here under the witness, it was then said by Judge Antonetti and not by Mr. Praljak. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Judge Prandler is quite right. Nothing escapes my attention. Line 3, page 52, I was speaking, not you. I'll go over it again. You said a minute ago that Colonel Siljeg had been interviewed by the OTP and that there were three or four binders on the subject. You are very familiar with the situation. You said that there were three or four binders. I assume that you've read through what Colonel Siljeg said. What did he say about this document, as far as you can remember, because I don't know what he said. I don't have any control over the disclosure of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, I can't remember that Mr. Siljeg was asked anything about this subject, although I was asked about this a few years ago, when the lengthy interview of Mr. Siljeg was completed. I hoped that he would be a Prosecution witness. You don't want members of the fire brigade to testify against a general. So I don't remember this subject being discussed, and I doubt that Siljeg could have provided a relevant answer, because he never had such a text before him, the handwriting of this kind before him. If anything reached him, I don't know if anything reached him, but if anything did reach him, he can then say whether that concerned me or not. I wasn't in Mostar on the 10th. I arrived on the 11th. But I believe that the OTP should confirm my thesis. The OTP should bring Siljeg here, not me. I dispute this document, the entire document. So an expert in handwriting should testify. If I'd been there, why wouldn't I have signed it? And the document is signed by someone else. Well, I also sign them. I don't know how to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have two documents. You can note in P1969, the first document, that there is a stamp, and this stamp, well, it's 2025 hours, the 2nd of May. The number is 2640. The second document that the Prosecution showed you was registered at -- well, on the same day, apparently, at 2125 hours. The number is 2641. When one has a look at the two stamps, one might think that the person who filed the two documents was the very same person, because the handwriting appears to be identical. You say that the second document, "Brada," is false. That means that the first document is also false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that the handwriting is the same, but neither of the documents has anything to do with me. This was written with some kind of a Siemens heading. Well, I don't know. How can I answer that? Siemens, what's that, where's that from? Siemens isn't contained on the first one. The second one has a reference to the Siemens. HVO had a heading of its own. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you have lawyers defending you. I don't know, but a lawyer who does his work is familiar or is aware of the fact that there is a false document. It would be necessary to send a letter to Mr. Siljeg, and one should say, On the 10th of May you sent a document number 01432. Although this goes -- although this took place a long time ago, you demanded for the artillery to intervene. Your lawyer could then send a copy of the document to Siljeg. Siljeg would have a look at the relevant document, and he either remembers it or not. If he doesn't remember it, he says, No, I can't answer your question, or he can remember it and he says, I never sent this document, or, I did send the document. So that's how one should proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Siljeg sends his request to the Main Staff. He can say, Fine, I sent that, but that has nothing to do with the response, that has nothing to do with me. Siljeg was probably in Rama, and the person who sent this from Mostar or who included this false document is in Mostar, and Siljeg could then say he has nothing to do with these documents. Siljeg is in Rama, and someone sent this from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, if we accept that Colonel Siljeg sent the document well at the time, he must know who the duty officer was -- he must have known who the duty officer was in the command. So, in theory --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How should he know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps he doesn't know but in theory, so he could say I can't say anything or he could say I remember it was lieutenant such and such or captain such and such, you should see about it with him. That's how one proceeds with an investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he had no telephone line to the duty officer. This was sent by packet communications. He had no idea who would receive it. He received a response that someone had concluded that it was attributed to me falsely. So these were two men communicating at a distance through packet communications as to who sent this, as to whether he sent this, how this arrived, there are two sentences; "Brada," and Slobodan Praljak, and this has nothing to do with Slobodan Praljak or with Brada. I don't know how this was done, so an expert in handwriting should be provided with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may contribute to the discussion. With all due respect, I don't agree with your advice as to what the Defence should have done or could have done. We have examined this document very carefully. I'd like to remind you that we informed the Chamber, in a submission before General Praljak started testifying, we informed the Chamber about the documents we believed were false documents, and this document was included in the list. The Defence has been claiming that this document is a false one. This has been a continual claim. We are aware of this from the earlier preparations that were made. As Defence counsel, we know what sort of a case this is. We believe that when we say that a document is a false document, the Prosecution has the burden of proof. It is for the OTP to prove that the document is authentic. The OTP asked the Accused Praljak about it. Perhaps the OTP could have asked a second, a fifth, a fifteenth expert or witness about this, or an expert in handwriting. As to whether they'd acted in this way or not, that's the Prosecution's problem. The document, according to what the witness has said, is not authentic. And then, Your Honour, there's one other very important thing, and this is also one of the reasons for which we decided not to pursue the matter. All the documents under P10936, the two handwritten documents and the alleged packet communications document, don't have an origin. They're not from the Croatian Archives because they don't bear the stamp of the Croatian Archives. This means that the Prosecution received these documents from someone or someone included these in some kind of packet of documents from Bosnia and Herzegovina or from Croatia. We can't know anything about this. You had established a threshold -- the Chamber established a threshold, and from the outset we've been trying to establish authenticity, but authenticity has not been proved here. This threshold hasn't been reached. A threshold that would prove the authenticity of the document hasn't been reached here. And earlier on, with regard to the first document which General Praljak allegedly signed himself, originally the number was P2280 and now the number is P10936, the first page of the original, you dismissed this earlier in one of your decisions because you can't receive any information -- or you haven't received any information on its authenticity. You have heard the answers, the witness is testifying. I am not testifying. All I can say is that with all due respect, Your Honours, the Defence took a rational decision and decided that it wasn't necessary to call Siljeg or to present other evidence. The OTP has the burden of proof. The Prosecution must say, Praljak, you wrote this. Praljak says, No, I didn't. The Prosecution can't even prove the authenticity of the document now. So, Your Honours, if there's no firm evidence to show that the document is authentic, and if we can't demonstrate the source, well, in that case I believe that in this courtroom we should waste no more time on the matter, now that the witness has provided his answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Praljak, please go ahead. We'll wait for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would perhaps be best if you took the floor once Mr. Praljak has returned. We'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, the Defence position is clear, and it's always been consistent. They've been saying that it's a false document. We accept that it's the Prosecution's burden, as the proponent -- as the party that's offering the document, that we have to prove sufficiently to the Trial Chamber that it's authentic. We believe we have, and that's, in part, what's happening here. Ultimately, it's for the Trial Chamber to decide whether there are sufficient indications that the document is authentic. And it's the Prosecution's submission that there are ample indications of that found, first of all, in the stamps of the HVO Main Staff that indicate, in our view, the document is authentic as being within the HVO Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Pardon me, pardon me. [Interpretation] I apologise, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would like to finish making my submissions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that it is now argument. This is going in final brief, what you are telling us now. What I said was only the procedural issue and directly a response to His Honour, the Judge, and now you are arguing why. There is a final brief you can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the document's being challenged as to authenticity. I'm saying he's saying that it's not authentic. He's saying it's handwritten and that it's not his handwriting. He's saying that we don't know the source. I'm pointing out, Mr. President, what the Prosecution believes are the things to the contrary that show that it is authentic. Ultimately, it's for the Trial Chamber to decide. It's got the stamps. The numbers line up. The stamps -- if you look at the Main Staff stamp in the Siljeg document, 9769, that's document 2640 if you look in the stamp. In the Praljak document, it's 2641. The Siljeg document comes in at 2045 p.m. The Praljak document goes out just about one hour later or less than an hour later at 2125. There are lots of indications of authenticity, the "Broj" numbers, the reference numbers, line up. Siljeg's incoming is reference number 432. Praljak's outgoing makes reference to document 432. It's all, in our view, Mr. President, sufficient indicia of authenticity. And I understand the Defence position. Ultimately, it's for the Trial Chamber to decide. And as to the source, as to the source, all documents are from the same source which were received from the HVO archive back to back in one, two, three, sequential order, as part of binder -- Main Staff HVO binder 12, number 696, and these were obtained by Mr. Prelec of the Office of the Prosecutor from the Croatian State Archive on the 13th of September of the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours, that's impossible. The Prosecution can tell us about the source of its documents in any way it deems fit, but the Prosecution, and that's what we have done, too, has argued in this case and in other cases, and they have also brought witnesses in to explain the process in previous cases. I'll also be calling a witness, a 92 bis witness, who will describe the technology, the process. But if a document has been received from the Croatian Archives, and that's the only place where HVO documents were found or HZ-HB documents were found, if that's the case, it has to have an archival emblem, a small circular stamp initially and then a square stamp subsequently. Your Honours, I'd like to remind you of the fact that you refused -- or you didn't allow the Defence to use many documents because the source wasn't the archives. You accepted many documents as authentic documents, and you said that the source was not in dispute. It was the Croatian Archives. But if Mr. Prelec, the Prosecution investigator, obtained these in some other way before the documents were provided to the state archives, well, in that case the Prosecution has to state very precisely where the documents were found, with whom, were they provided with the documents by an agency, by someone in authority, by some special intermediary, or were the documents obtained from the original archives or from the archives that subsequently became the state archives. There's no authenticity here, and that's the end of the matter. The Prosecution cannot say, In my books, it says such and such a thing. That's not sufficient. And I apologise. Just one more sentence, Your Honour, just one more sentence, if I may. In the Cerkez-Kordic case, the Prosecution called four witnesses in order to explain or demonstrate the authenticity of the video of the -- of the federal or so-called presidential transcripts, let's say non-authenticity, rather, and Mr. Prelec spoke about how the documents were taken from the archives at the same time. This was at the outset. Later, the process changed somewhat. But there has to be a stamp. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, just a minor detail. You are quite right, the document P9769 has a small stamp in the B/C/S version. However, in the document signed "Brada," handwritten, I can't see a stamp. There's no small stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I agree, Mr. President. I mean, it's evident whether any of these contains a stamp or it doesn't. I don't have anything to add on that. The Prosecution's made its submissions as to this document or this series of documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will see about this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing, if I may. We don't dispute the authenticity of 9769. There may be such documents. It seems to be quite appropriate. It bears the stamp. We don't dispute this. We're only disputing the authenticity of the two documents that allegedly are Praljak documents, or rather the three documents, because there's the packet communications document, the authenticity of which we also challenge. It doesn't bear a stamp. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P4325, 4325, staying with the issue of command climate. I think -- well, I know we've seen this document at an earlier stage of your testimony. I don't believe that you challenge its authenticity. Am I correct in that? This is one of your documents dated "Prozor, 16 August 1993"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, this is one of my documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is from the time in which you were the commander of the HVO Main Staff; correct? 16 August.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you're sending this from Prozor down to the HVO Main Staff and also to the Command of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone in Tomislavgrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in this document, General, you're going through and you're making an assessment or a listing of the various HVO units, their numerical strength within the various units, and they're all listed there. I'm not going to go through them all. And then you say, at the bottom of page 2 of the English, that it's necessary to deduct 10 per cent for various reasons, such as wounding, et cetera, exhaustion. You say that there is -- the only good-quality unit capable of carrying out an attack is near Filipovici, that they are -- they, too, are supposed to leave the Rama area in keeping with a verbal order. And then after that paragraph, you simply say, Fuck it, in English. Now, General, recognising that you were extremely frustrated at the time that you wrote this document, again, if we're going to talk about the command climate that you're trying to set, even at a time when perhaps things aren't going so well for the HVO, militarily, down in Herceg-Bosna, when the commander of the Main Staff, especially when it's someone like you, with your background coming from the Croatian Government and Croatian Army, makes such a statement here and sends it down the chain of command to the operative zone and the Main Staff, the command climate or the signal that's being sent is one of extreme unprofessionalism, at best; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. If -- they swear anywhere. They swear in the American Army. In wartime, every army swears. I didn't send this as you say. Well, you said -- you always add the operation zones. I only sent this to the operation zone and the Main Staff in Mostar, only to high-ranking officers, to myself, that's correct, because I wanted to see how many troops we, in fact, had, not to see how many we had according to the various lists in existence. And it's correct that in such a situation, 21 units didn't have more than 2.100, 2.200 men. That's about 100 men per unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, but I'm not challenging the data contained in the document. I don't think you answered my question. You're commander of the Main Staff, General. It's not professional for you to use language like that in a document that you're sending down to your Main Staff and to your operative zone; isn't that true? Are you going to defend this language?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will defend it. It's quite understandable, in such a situation, and this can be found in many statements given by various commanders in all armies. You have worse language than this, similar language. I stand by what I said. I know the situation I was in. I know what this meant. When I said, Fuck it, we have to survive, as to how we are to survive, I had no idea. I was to meet with those 21 units, run from one to the other with my commanders, try to get the most from them after an intense Muslim offensive, so I don't see anything wrong with this. Military language isn't established. It's not as if there was a professional and non-professional military language in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next one I'm going to talk about is or I'm going to ask you about is the language contained in your -- your order that was issued in connection with events that were taking place in Vares in October of 1993. And I don't have it in the binder, but it's a well-known document. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we proceed to the next document, I would like to focus on something else. Mr. Praljak, there's here a list of units and soldiers. I note that in the Prozor-Gornji Vakuf zone there are 4.424 persons. 10 per cent are not operative for various reasons. Let us say there were roughly 4.000. So I would like to broach another question. I have already asked you this question, and I come back to it. With 4.000 soldiers, can one attack the ABiH? What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not, Your Honour, except that your accounting is not right. I say that 10 per cent are for various reasons out of combat, but then the other people from Jajce were absolutely exhausted, then units from Sebesic, which the ABiH captured a long time ago. So 40 per cent of the people of Sebesic army are mentally ill. Some had then fled, part of people from Bugojanci, then the 5th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army, only 130 infantrymen were left. This is an authentic document from the field, when I was on the verge of complete failure, on the edge of losing territory. Then the Zrinski Battalion consists of 38 men. So the people of Klica, they are not there either. So at this point in time, I didn't have more than 2.100 or 2.200 soldiers. I'm sorry, I'm speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that you had 2.000 or 2.100 or 2.200 soldiers, and with these soldiers you had to confront the Serbs and the ABiH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, from Raduski Kamen to the left, at least 40 [Realtime transcript read in error "2.000 or 3.000 metres"] or 50 kilometres of some sort of a line had to be maintained. And if you looked at the forces of the ABiH that were attacking, then this was extremely difficult when people were absolutely on the verge of their abilities, and we managed somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I think it is not translated at all. It's not translated at all, what Mr. Praljak has said. I heard, for instance, "50 kilometres," and it's not part of transcript. Maybe the best way is for Mr. Praljak to repeat once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, apparently you said something very quickly that has not been registered in the transcript. You mentioned 50 kilometres, and we don't see it in the text. What exactly did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This remaining manpower of 2.100 or 2.200 men were defending a front-line that was 50 to 60 kilometres long, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, these 2.100 men that you had under your command here, they had to defend a front-line which was at least 60 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifty to sixty kilometres, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you know, the Muslims, what was their strength?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The smallest ratio was 1:5, 1:6, or even more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Very briefly, the actual issue while this document has come up was the last two words there, and you have said that this was usual also in other armies. Do you have any example of a written order of a supreme commander, or chief, general chief of staffs, that uses such language? You have said that this was usual. I wonder whether you have any example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that it was customary in my case. I said that it was not unusual to use this kind of language in all armies. It is not customary in my case, but it reflects an extremely difficult situation. Simply, there's no army left, and this is my letter asking to see what our real forces were. Your Honour, I could look up to find various orders from commanders, from Patton, who would slap his men if he thought that they were faking the reasons for not going to the front, then some of Napoleon's generals, then, not to mention about the Russian Army and their commanders. So if you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have spoken now about slapping. One day here in court you have also said that hypothetically you might have beaten someone. I think I leave it at that. Thank you. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, if you'll turn to the next document, which should be P06028. This is dated the 23rd of October, 1993, from the HVO Main Staff forward command post at Citluk. It's issued to a lot of different offices and people, as we can see they are both in Kiseljak and in Vitez, the Main Staff, Petkovic, Mario Bradara, Ivica Rajic, Kordic, Blaskic, on the solution of problems in Vares. And, General, we've talked about this one before. You say: "Sort out the situation in Vares showing no mercy towards anyone. Find people who are up to both the times and the task." Now, General, earlier in your testimony on the 23rd of June of this year, you indicated that you wrote the original of this to General Petkovic only, and that you were not issuing the orders to anyone other than Petkovic. You say on line 25 of page 41870: "Well, the thing is very simple. I didn't write anything to Rajic, or the Bobovac Brigade, or anybody else. I did not issue orders to them, to not Rajic or Bobovac Brigade ever. I wrote to General Petkovic the original document after I had received multiple reports about disorder in Vares, smuggling, Harez [phoen], adverse situation. There were five, seven, even more reports. It was then that I wrote General Petkovic, and I wrote to him. Petkovic, I'm not issuing him orders. I'm writing Petkovic and then the text, 'Put the situation in Vares in order without any mercy.'" Now, General, first of all, this document shows -- 6028, that, in fact, you were not directing these remarks exclusively to General Praljak, but in fact you were -- your intention was to distribute this text and these orders widely to the Command of the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade and to Ivica Rajic, and to the other people shown on here; isn't that true? It wasn't intended just for Petkovic; it was intended for much wider distribution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. General Matic signed this, so he rewrote my original document and sent it to these people. It is not an order. It is a solution of the problems in Vares. I don't know why I would send such a solution to them, but let me make myself quite clear. I don't mind that this was sent to the others. I didn't do it, but why not? Never mind, let them solve the problem in Vares without any connections, who is whose relative, who is being lenient towards who because of smuggling, et cetera. So this is not an order. It is a logical addressed to my deputy, Petkovic, Deal with it up there and find men, of course Croatian men, who would deal with these people. That is the original idea. It could have been sent to Blaskic, it could have been sent to whoever you like, but that is the position behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: These are your words. I know you say General Matic sent this. These are your words; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, those are my words, and that is what I would say even today, Deal with them, arrest them. It's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you don't say, Arrest them. In fact, you don't say anything other than to show no mercy. So what you've done here, General, is leave open to interpretation of anyone seeing this that, in fact, they can take whatever measures they deem necessary to sort out the situation in Vares; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When you say "without mercy," that means within legal frameworks. If you believe that when we say, No mercy, means cutting off people's heads or dealing brutally with people, then you should have found in my documents or in my actions that this could mean anything else but; putting an end to their smuggling, laziness, bad actions, lack of discipline, and deal with them without mercy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, this doesn't even indicate who's to be sorted out, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic was down there. He was familiar with the documents as well as I was. He knew what the situation was like, and he knows exactly -- exactly what this refers to. This is completely clear to my deputy because it was not the first time for us to discuss this, and the documents coming from the area of Vares regarding problems with the brigade commanders, he was familiar with all that. And it is true that I had had enough of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There were also a lot of other problems that the HVO was having at this time; isn't that true, General? They were having big problems with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Muslims who were in Vares; isn't that also true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This relates to Croats only, to find the people who would put some order into things and who would be up to the times and the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You show us where, in this order, it says that this relates to Croats only.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you need to remove someone from his position, showing no mercy, and you also have to find people who would be up to the tasks and the times, and you're removing someone from the HVO, then who will you find to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, the point is that, in fact, this document doesn't say anything about dealing with Croats or removing people from their positions. It's an open-ended order on your part, as commander of the Main Staff, which really can be interpreted by anyone receiving it as in any way that they saw fit. Don't you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't agree. If you need to find someone who are up to doing something, and you're talking about the HVO, then there's only one logical interpretation: That you will find people, Croats, who would be up to the times to carry this out, so as to settle the situation in Vares, and which people who need to be removed without mercy are to blame for. And if you can give any other interpretation, that is absolutely illogical. This can only have one interpretation when one respects logic. But if you do not respect logic, then you can interpret it in any way you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The timing of this -- with this story you're giving us about the smuggling, the timing is hard to accept. You say you've been receiving multiple reports about disorder in Vares, smuggling up there. You're unhappy with certain people in the HVO civilian government, and yet you pick this particular time, the 23rd of October, to deal with the problem of smuggling. I find that hard to believe, in light of everything else that was happening in Vares at this same point in time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you're skipping over key documents and you extract something, then you can claim whatever you wish. This is a document that I signed because, according to the report I had received, Duznovic had been arrested, then the deputy brigade commander had also been replaced, but if you were to show the original document, which you are avoiding to do because I'm afraid that your aim is not to establish the truth but to win at all cost, show us the original document and you will see what it says. And His Honour Judge Antonetti has already asked me about it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me take you to the next document. I'm going to move forward in time. This is, again, your -- P06051, P06051. This is a document written by a duty officer named Zorinko Bosnjak, and he's sitting in the Command of the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak at 4.00 in the morning on the 24th of October, 1993. Colonel Rajic is down in Vares at this point in time; correct, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, this is going from the command of the brigade in Kiseljak down to the Bobovac Brigade in Vares, and it's directed personally to Colonel Rajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this duty officer is informing Rajic about some communications that had taken place with the XY side. Do we agree, General, that the XY side reference here is a reference to the Serb armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then this duty officer is then passing on to Colonel Rajic also information, and I'll read it: "We received an information from Major General Slobodan Praljak stating that continuous active operations are executed in the last three days in the Gornji Vakuf area, and that we occupied Brenovac, Oglavak, and parts of Bistrica, and that we move along, as well as an order for Vares: 'The situation in Vares has to be resolved showing no mercy to anyone. Find men able to cope with the moment and the assignments." So, General, now what we see is that your words -- these words are moving down the chain of command, which is how they should be treated, coming from the commander of the HVO Main Staff, through the brigade headquarters in Kiseljak, down to the brigade -- the Bobovac Brigade down in Vares, down to the ranking officer down there, Colonel Rajic, and in fact it's become such -- it's a document or -- I should say your words now are being communicated along by people at the level of Zorinko Bosnjak, who's a low-level operations officer, who is sitting there at the communications desk at 4.00 in the morning. So, General, can we agree that your words on Vares, whatever their intent, your words are moving steadily down the chain of command and being disseminated, as you intended, to a number of people who are present in Vares?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say that it's an order, and that is not right. What I sent was not an order. You say, As you wish. That is not correct either. I just sent two sentences to General Petkovic. It's not an order. My wish is crystal clear, but every crystal clear wish can be interpreted in various ways, if people wish to do so. And here also, when I talk about dealing with the situation in Vares, showing no mercy and to find the people up to the task and assignment, and if a lower-level officer has some doubts as to how the order can be interpreted, he must ask the higher command what was meant if he didn't understand it. And if someone were to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we move into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just -- one very, very brief thing. I would kindly ask Judge Trechsel to check the transcript on the break, of course, so we are not here, your last words in transcript on page 67, line 10. I understand something is wrong. It was either wrongly interpreted or you understood wrongly the response by Mr. Praljak. Please, sir, check and see what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go into private session, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we've been looking at this last document in respect of Vares. And just to round this off, General, when we talk about your language on showing no mercy, or whether you use language like the "F" word, as I'll put it, the Prosecution puts it to you that you did, in fact, give Colonel Siljeg the green light to flatten Jablanica, which is what he wanted to do, as indicated in the document we've just looked at a few minutes ago. General, when you use language like that, and also the earlier document from January 1993, Gornji Vakuf, where you said that they'd be annihilated or flattened or crushed, when you use open-ended incendiary language like that, you can count on crimes happening, isn't that true, because the soldiers whom you command require specificity and they require to be -- to have a commander who acts and communicates with them in a professional manner; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me. You've mentioned five documents now, the ones that I dispute to and the one containing the term used by Siljeg. I say that it's not a term that I used. I stand by two words used, and that concerns the list of men. That's what I used, that's the language I used, and what I said to General Petkovic is language I used, but the sense was quite the contrary. If you believe that this is incendiary language sent to General Petkovic, well, the sense is, in fact, quite the reverse. In order to prevent what partially happened probably up there, I said, Petkovic, replace them, take action, and don't pay attention to who --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I don't agree with anything you have said. I've provided you with full explanations, and however much you insist on other interpretations, these should remain your interpretations, but I have exhaustively answered all the questions you have put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's your position, sir, that your orders, as reflected in these documents, meets the standards of professionalism and lawfulness that should apply to orders issued by commanders at your level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I issued these two orders, or, rather, the comment, I gave a comment, I never issued an order of that kind. What you have been referring to, you're referring to it as an order, but it doesn't say "order" anywhere, so I don't understand this. Where did you read the word "order" in the document to Petkovic? There's no "order." You'll continue to repeat the word "order" 100 times. I'm telling you, it wasn't an order. On numerous occasions, and witnesses have testified about this, I have also addressed the matter, I acted with the utmost professionalism, and often I took stringent action to prevent a lack of order. Sometimes it was necessary to risk one's life to solve problems, it was necessary to use ours, but this was done only to prevent crimes from being committed. This has been demonstrated scores of times here, and there's nothing else I can add.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But, in fact, the language that you sent to Vares, whether we characterise it as an order, or an instruction, or a request, it was, in fact, interpreted by your subordinates, including the subordinates on the ground in Vares, as an order, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even if they had interpreted it as an order -- well, they should have interpreted it as it was written. Replace the idiots and those who are carrying out poor work so that we can solve the situation in a military, adequate way, that's what it says. It says replace the Croats who have contributed to this negative situation, and this concerned the military and organisational system, structure. There were poor defence lines, the system was poorly organised. Yes, thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree, however, that this last document on show no mercy doesn't say anything about replacing people, it doesn't say anything about the idiots that you're referring to here; it simply says, Show no mercy and sort out the situation in Vares?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stringer, to whom? If it says find men, then I said, Remove the idiots and find men to deal with the situation. Look, really --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object to the questions put by Mr. Stringer. And, please, could the general be shown the document with his original handwriting? In this courtroom, we've already heard the general say, on a number of occasions -- or tell us about how things actually unfolded on a number of occasions. Could we just show the original document to the general, the document containing his handwriting, and then we can proceed with all the other questions, because if we just extract this one sentence and interpret it as an order, if we just do that, the Chamber won't have a full or a complete idea of how things unfolded, and you won't understand what the message to General Petkovic concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've seen the other document. I'm less interested in that one. I'm interested in the version that went down the chain of command. I think the issue has been exhausted in the general's direct examination as well as in the questions that came from the President, so I don't see any need to go back to the original document when the ones that we're interested in, for this purposes, relates to the chain of command and how it impacted the chain of command. I'm ready to move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, your witness [as interpreted] says that if you are to answer the questions, one should show you the text containing this sentence of yours. Is this necessary for you or not? If not, we'll continue with the questions. So you are testifying, not your Defence counsel. Do you think it's necessary to have a look at the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. You've already asked me about that text. You have it before you. Everything is quite clear here. I've answered all the questions. Everything is clear to me. I can repeat to the same extent that the Prosecution can repeat its thesis. I'll continue to repeat my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're going to switch gears a little bit now, and I'm going to ask you some questions about the HVO Main Staff from 24th of July, 1993, in terms of just how it worked in a general sense or an organisational sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the question is posed, I'm sitting here and I do feel the obligation, at least as an officer of the Court, to make one observation for the Trial Chamber, and that is: When counsel for an accused, even as one as brilliant as General Praljak is, stands up and makes an observation, as was done just now, and believes that in fairness to the record and to her client, that a particular document should be shown, I think the better practice is not to ask the witness what he or she thinks, because the witness may not necessarily be in the best position to understand the intricacies involved in this particular case or the issues that are being discussed, and therefore I think the better practice would be to defer to counsel and not to ask the witness whether the witness feels it would be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel has access to the documents. Counsel can see the document. The Prosecution said, We'll move on to another area, so that's the end of the discussion. Had the Prosecution continued, we would have taken your objection into account, but Mr. Stringer is moving on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the sake of the transcript, I would like it to be known that you didn't see the document that's being discussed all day today. You've only had the document before you, the document that someone copied at one moment in time. The document with Mr. Praljak's original handwriting isn't one that you have seen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Nika, when I said I didn't need it, well, I've just had enough. That's why we've spent so many hours trying to do something that, in my opinion, has no sense, because my text is crystal clear to me, but everything else, well, to be quite frank, I leave it to fate. I don't really have the desire to discuss these matters. The message to General Petkovic was crystal clear, crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. I have to intervene for another reason. I was waiting for the Prosecution to complete his questions with regard to this area, with regard to the context of the entire series of questions, starting with a statement made by the expert witness, General Pringle, and then going on to the documents that we have examined. With regard to this, I would like it to be stated quite clearly in the transcript by the Prosecution that the indictment isn't being amended, because the indictment refers to this document, the message Praljak sent to Petkovic, and it refers to it in a different context. The questions put to the witness provide me with a dilemma. Is the Prosecution now trying to establish a basis so that the Prosecution could argue that Praljak -- and I'm exaggerating a bit, but are they claiming that Praljak acted incautiously when he allowed himself to use a certain kind of language in a certain number of documents, and as a result he provoked his subordinates to think in a certain way? We started with General Pringle, but did he create such a command climate? Is the Prosecution now insinuating -- has the Prosecution been insinuating for the last two hours of its cross-examination that Praljak used this language in order to send a message to his men, and in this way he caused them to act erroneously? When we follow the series of questions put to the witness, I believe that the Prosecution might be making new charges, and I'd like the Prosecution to state that this is not the case, to state that the indictment isn't being amended, if that's the case. Perhaps it's not the case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, you will answer the question, but I'll try and summarise what has been said to you. You've provided a number of examples in which Mr. Praljak used language, certain written terms in documents, and as a result of this language, the use of these terms, he might not have created the kind of command climate that the expert, General Pringle, referred to in his report. The expert says that it's necessary for there to be a good climate so that command can be adequately exercised. A certain number of examples were provided, and you asked Mr. Praljak whether using swear words, using certain language, you asked him whether using such language had an effect on soldiers, on his men. Is that what you wanted to demonstrate, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm troubled that I've been -- I think I've been putting the Prosecution case on this to the witness most of today, and if nobody understands that, then I've been doing a pretty bad job of it. The Prosecution case is that by the documents and the orders and the language of General Praljak we've been talking about, he created a command climate in which his subordinates felt free to commit crimes or to approve crimes or to look the other way and tolerate crimes. That's our submission. If I could just add, because I don't understand counsel's remarks. I don't think I should have the obligation to explain what I'm doing to counsel or to respond to every inquiry they want to make about the cross-examination. They're going to have redirect, and the general is here to answer the questions. I'm not here to answer questions of the Defence. They're not objecting. They're simply asking for clarifications and explanations, which I think I don't have to provide. I'm just doing my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, of course, of course, I do not expect the Prosecution, nor can I have any such expectations, for them to explain their line of questioning or where they're heading. That was not my intention, I assure you. But the Prosecution has again repeated something that is disturbing. [In English] "The documents and the orders and the language of General Praljak we have been talking about, he created a command climate in which his subordinates felt free to commit crimes or to approve crimes." [Interpretation] That is a new factual description in the indictment and it is a new charge. We do not have such insinuations in the indictment, this incrimination expressed in this way, such a factual situation and such a legal interpretation. We really don't have that indictment, or I don't recollect it properly. And, furthermore, my learned friend has not provided an answer that I can accept. Let him say, No, they are not new charges, or let him say, Yes, they are new charges. What my learned friend said regarding explaining the line of the cross-examination, that is something I fully accept. Of course, he is not duty-bound to explain that. But let him answer my question: Are they new charges or not? A simple yes-or-no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer, are they new charges or charges already contained in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is all evidence that's highly probative and relevant in our view to the issue of the general's command responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no answer, so I can presume as a Defence that there are no new charges. I'm just -- I'm simply trying to avoid a situation in which, in a couple -- next months, the Prosecution will write in the final brief this situation, why Praljak is responsible for something. I just understand that there are no new charges, that it is not a new form of liability, neither the facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just for the record, we are going to write in our brief and in our submissions that this sort of language that's in these orders give rise to a command climate which ultimately results in the general's criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3) for the crimes that are alleged in the indictment. I mean, there aren't any more -- any new crime bases, or I mean, we've been talking about Vares, the "flatten everything" related to the events just after the 9th of May in Jablanica. The one document was generated in Gornji Vakuf. So, I mean, there aren't any new crime locations or crime bases that we're adding. This all goes to the general's command responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3) for the crimes he's already charged with in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite clear, in paragraph 17(3) the following is written: "Slobodan Praljak participated in the commission of crimes and attacks by HVO forces against the Muslims of Bosnia, he incited their commission, he facilitated them, he encouraged them, and he tolerated them." Therefore, what you say, that is part of paragraph 17(3) that I have just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The -- that part of the indictment tracks along the very language of Article 7(1) and also perhaps 7(3), in terms of the bases for criminal responsibility under Article 7, and that's what this line of questioning has been relevant to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is not a new form of liability, it is already included. That is what we can draw as a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned friend upholds this position that he has just described, there is nothing new, that this is contained in the wording that you have read out, Your Honour, I'm simply referring to the existing practice, that is, the Kupreskic case in the Appeals Chamber, and I think Kvocka and Krnojelac - I'm not quite sure. That means that it is not a sufficiently specific charge. The one that has now been quoted is not specific enough for the Defence to be able to defend itself, because nowhere in the indictment is it explained that Praljak, by writing military documents and using free language in doing so, instigated the troops to commit crimes. That is a factual basis for such an indictment. That should be part of the indictment, according to established practice, regardless of how liberal it may be. The explanation given is not specific enough for an understanding of the indictment. The Statute requires that the accused must be informed in detail with the indictment, even though the Prosecution says that these are not new charges, but they are new charges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've spent already quite an amount of time on this subject. With the greatest respect, it seems that the position has been rather succinctly put by you, Mr. President, and it has been concurred with by my learned friends for the Prosecution. It seems that the submissions that may have -- that my learned friend for General Praljak and the Prosecution have on this issue are, indeed, best left to closing briefs and closing arguments, and they be determined by Your Honours in the final judgement. And, of course, they can always be revisited, if necessary, on appeal. But it doesn't appear to me to be an overly useful exercise to belabour this point any more than has already been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everyone has understood, and in your submissions you will elaborate on these matters. The Prosecution will respond, and the Defence also will comment, and then the Judges will rule. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, on the 6th of May, 2009, you were describing, in general terms, what I would refer to as a division of labour as between yourself and others after you took command of the Main Staff on the 24th of July, and I just want to ask you a couple of questions about that to make sure that I understand what you're saying correctly. And I'll just refer to a bit of the transcript from your testimony. You said: "At that moment, the commanders, myself, Petkovic, and the others, had to go to the field, leave their offices." And I'm skipping down a line. You say: "I understood, which will be corroborated by witnesses, that our main problem would be the attack by the BH Army from the direction of Uskoplje and Rama, which would have meant a complete defeat of the HVO, so I went there." And then you continue on. You say: "The area of Mostar and the south should have become the responsibility of the chief of General Staff." I think that's "chief of the Main Staff," and that's Brigadier Tole. And then, quote, you say: "General Petkovic was to concentrate on avoiding the fall of Kiseljak, Vares, and Central Bosnia." So, General, just to -- I want to clarify that I understand it correctly. During the time period of time that you were the commander of the HVO Main Staff, you were the commander and you were the highest-ranking military officer in the HVO structure. But if I understand correctly, based on this, there was something of a geographical division of labour as between you and General Petkovic and Brigadier Tole, as you've indicated here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an internal agreement or, rather, my request, for the simple reason that the situation -- if the situation is more chaotic, the possibility of managing it is more difficult; that is, an acting army or to acting as the Main Staff, for this could lead to a disaster. In such cases and in other wars, the commander cannot control the situation from one room in one location. In view of the strength of the attack of the ABiH, the situation with the HVO units that you have seen, the situation with the communications. And in a brief conversation -- Tole came a little later, so primarily it was between General Petkovic and me. The witnesses have testified about the main direction, which should have been Gornji Vakuf. I went there on the same day, and with a few days I fought for days and almost months, Mr. Petkovic had other obligations with UNPROFOR, the negotiations and so on. Of course, there was a certain division of labour, as I said, and I also explained the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn to Exhibit 3D01281 [Realtime transcript read in error "3D01821"]. That should be in your binder. This is one of your exhibits, 3D01281.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This from the "Croatian Soldier" magazine that you were talking about during one part of your direct examination. This issue is dated the 8th of May, 1992. Do you have that, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you referred us to this, you were talking about your activities in terms of educating the Croatian Army personnel on the Laws of War. And this -- this magazine actually contained what I thought was sort of a useful summary or resume of, as it's indicated here on page 2 of the English, the basic rules of International Law Applicable in Armed Conflict. This is page 0532 of your version. Do you have it? Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. In the transcript, it says "1821." It should be 3D01281, 1281.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That is correct. I apologise if I misspoke. 1281.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, General, we see in the box here text involving the basic rules of International Law Applicable in Armed Conflict, and we don't have to go through this point by point. But recognising that this is sort of an overview, would you agree with me that these, in general, set out the rules applicable and international -- excuse me, the rules that are applicable in armed conflict in respect of persons au de combat, civilians, captured combatants, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Soon after I took over as assistant minister, this was one of the first seminars on the Rules of War, and you can see listed some of the basic -- the most important rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that these rules applied to you at any time when you exercised command authority in connection with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when we talk about this division of labour, for example, when you were primarily responsible for the Prozor or Gornji Vakuf area and General Petkovic was looking after the Central Bosnia area, would you agree with me, General, that, in fact, these rules applied to you, you were responsible under these rules, you were responsible as the commander of the HVO Main Staff, even if something happened in one of the areas that General Petkovic was looking after?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense in which responsibility is proscribed by law, I was responsible even there, but if responsibility is interpreted in an absolutely broad sense, then I am responsible, too, as envisaged by the Law of Warfare; commanding, method of command, whether I had concealed something or not. Yes, I accept all kinds of responsibility as interpreted according to the Rules of War. Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whether I knew, whether I could have known. Even when I envisaged like sending to the church and so on, even more than was envisaged, I sought to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can ask the question this way, and maybe it will be better: You were not excused from your obligations simply by virtue of the fact that General Petkovic was looking after a different part of the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If something occurred due to my omission, my order, my intentions, my concealment, if anything may have happened as is written, I was commander of the Main Staff and certain responsibilities emanate from there, which I accept, but precisely in the way they are described in the books on international war law, and that was the practice in the trials of the American Army or any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that would also -- we've been talking about the Central Bosnia areas that General Petkovic looked after, but this would apply equally to the Mostar area and the area south of Mostar, which I understand Brigadier Tole was looking after?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is something I have already provided. I have already answered that question. A general is a general. A commander of the operative zone is the commander of an operative zone. If you think that one man can control all information under those conditions, or anything like that, let me repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, excuse me. Let me try to ask it the same way I asked for the other. For Mostar, the municipality, and for the HVO units that were deployed in Mostar and the areas south of Mostar, you were not excused of whatever applicability of international law there was simply because you were looking after Prozor and Gornji Vakuf; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you could turn to the next document. It's P00191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Stringer, and it's really an interruption. But as you are between two documents, perhaps you can live with it. I owe an answer to Mr. Kovacic about a passage in today's transcript which he has referred to and which we find on page 67, lines 10 to 12. I think that roughly the transcript is correct. After one -- "you have spoken now about slapping one," there should be a full stop, and the rest here in court should have a comma, so that the part here in court refers to what comes afterwards. And the basis of this is actually a bit -- a bit more concrete, if you want, and I'm here referring on the transcript of our hearing on page 39481 of 4th May, lines 4 to 6, where Mr. Praljak is reported as saying: "As for members of my own people, on various occasions I would swear and yell over and above any civilised norm of behaviour. Sometimes I would even hit a person." That was what I had remembered and what I refer to, and I hope that you are satisfied with this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is quite so. Thank you, Your Honour. That is what I thought it was, but it wasn't clear from the transcript because one could possibly interpret it as if at that particular moment when your comment was transcribed, that you understood that the slap General Praljak mentioned, that was done by General Patton during the Second World War, so that is why I made the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for having given me the opportunity to clarify this. And excuse me, Mr. Stringer, for having interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have two questions. Within the framework of what General Petkovic said a moment ago, when I look at the document about "Croatian Soldiers," this magazine, this document was at the level of the Republic of Croatia. However, to the best of your knowledge, was this document conveyed to the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The document was shown of the IPD when he testified here, and this document says, We're not receiving Croatian soldiers, or, rather, in smaller numbers, can you do anything about it, that is number one. And, secondly, the booklets with the Red Cross were sent to the HVO and everyone had them. The magazine, "Croatian Soldier," was distributed free at all levels of the HVO and the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that this publication was distributed free of charge, and the first page shows that the price was 100 dinars. Why is this indicated? Why does it say "100 HRD"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because at kiosks for the population, for the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the population who wanted to buy one they had to pay for it. I see. So this document was distributed among soldiers and you tell us that HVO soldiers had one. The one from May 1992, when one turns the page and focuses on page 4, we see that there was a seminar organised by the International Red Cross, because we see the emblem there, and in a large square there are certain legal rules that were passed down to the soldiers; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. And you see at the end, in the announcement for the media that I headed, the Red Cross told us that they wished to do the same with the former Yugoslav Army because they were not convinced that they were acting appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does it mean that the foot soldier, the lowest-level soldier, at least who can read, can see that parties at conflict must distinguish between the civilian population and combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, all of them, not only on the basis of this magazine, but from the booklet that was distributed to each soldier in the HVO and the HV, including pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question, but the Prosecutor will return to it tomorrow because it's almost 7.00. You said something that interested me a lot. You said it before, but I didn't intervene straight away. But you said that, in reality, you distributed responsibility among three of you; you, Petkovic and Tole. Each one had a separate zone. And I thought this was interesting, but you are confirming that all three of you shared this responsibility. Mr. Stringer said that even if you did have this division of labour, does this mean that you assume your own responsibility as the hierarchal superior, even though this is rather a complicated point. On the basis of a verbal agreement between Tole, Petkovic, and you, you distributed the geographical zones, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, and Petkovic also had talks with UNPROFOR, with the ABiH. He continued his own activities. And, secondly, of course I am responsible if I fail to react to anything being done wrongly by Petkovic or Tole, and everyone else, of course. In the conditions that we had, in view of the communications we had, and the kind of war that was ongoing, if anyone could prove that I violated any provision of International Law, I am ready to bear full responsibility for this, and I said that at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it's 7.00 p.m., actually several minutes after 7.00, and I apologise to the interpreters. As you know, we will be working in the afternoon, and we will resume our hearing at a quarter past 2.00. And I wish you all a good evening.
